title: Information Bias
hook: Another report can feel like progress even after the deciding fact is already on the table.
counterintuition: More data does not automatically mean a better decision. Information bias starts when extra facts feel useful without changing the comparison that matters.
tryThisNow: Before asking for one more number, write the choice in two options and name the fact that would actually switch your answer.
keyTakeaway: Useful information changes the decision; decorative information only postpones responsibility.

breakdown.fastRead:
The airport board above Julian's diamond booth flashes delayed flights from Antwerp and Dubai. A buyer has made a first offer, and Julian wants another market sheet before responding. His assistant points to the spread already on the desk. Julian marks information bias on the board and writes the switching fact: a comparable stone sold above today's offer.

Information bias pulls you to collect more after the key test is clear. Facts can help. The next fact must be able to change the choice.

A fact that cannot move the decision is a delay wearing a badge.
breakdown.deepRead:
The airport board gives Julian a perfect excuse to wait. More flights mean more brokers. More brokers mean more possible prices. But his decision is narrower: accept the first offer, counter, or walk. The relevant comparison is the offer against current comparable stones, not every whisper from every arriving dealer. He writes decision relevance beside the board and stops the search at the fact that could change his answer.

Information bias feels responsible because it avoids the embarrassment of deciding too soon. A person asks for one more survey, one more dashboard, one more test, one more expert note. Sometimes that is exactly right. Missing information can be fatal. But the bias begins when the next fact has no clear job. It will not choose between the options. It will only make the chooser feel less exposed.

More data can become a hiding place.

Tomas sees the same pattern in a language school placement office. A loan worksheet lies under the level-test results because the school wants to sell a premium course. The student already scored clearly into intermediate. Tomas marks decision relevance on the worksheet and refuses to request a third oral interview unless it could move the student into a different level.

A stopping rule protects the decision from endless appetite. Before gathering more, state what result would make you act differently. If no possible result changes the action, stop. If several results would matter, gather those and ignore the rest. The rule is not anti-curiosity. It is respect for the choice in front of you.
breakdown.fullRead:
The tasting spoon in Niels's food bank warehouse has dried lentil soup on its edge. A storm is closing two roads, and three trucks have to be assigned before noon. A volunteer asks for updated household preference surveys before loading anything. Niels marks more data on the spoon and names the comparison: which route can deliver calories safely today. Preferences matter for planning next month, but they will not decide which truck can cross the bridge in two hours.

Information bias often arrives in humane clothing. You want to be fairer, safer, more accurate. You do not want to dismiss a detail that might matter. This is why the correction has to be concrete. Ask the decision to name its missing comparison. Then ask whether the next information source can change that comparison. If it cannot, the search is no longer serving the decision.

What would you do differently if the answer came back high, low, or unchanged?

Jonathan Baron, Jane Beattie, and John C. Hershey examined heuristics and biases in diagnostic reasoning, including how congruent information and certainty can distort judgment. The medical pressure is easy to recognize: extra test results can make a diagnosis feel firmer even when they do not distinguish between the live possibilities. A doctor needs information that separates the competing diseases, not information that simply adds weight to a favorite story.

You can use that discipline in ordinary work. Brielle sits in a tenant-complaint meeting with a scoreboard still from a building camera. The landlord wants another week of noise logs before deciding whether to repair a loose service door. Brielle marks stopping rule on the still and asks what new log entry would change the action. None would. The visible door slam is enough to schedule the repair.

Information can be useful later and irrelevant now. That distinction saves time without insulting the data. A bike-share team may want weather, speed, rider age, pavement type, and truck delivery records. Maeve, reviewing a crash hotspot with a shipping manifest on the table, separates two questions. For today's bollard placement, crash location and turning path matter. For next quarter's fleet design, the manifest may matter. She marks useful information beside the manifest and refuses to let a future question stall a present fix.

The danger is not ignorance. The danger is collecting facts that make you feel less ignorant while leaving the decision untouched.

Robin sees the postmortem version in a payroll bonus test. The ad mockup for the internal launch had been reviewed twelve times. HR kept requesting more engagement data before choosing between a flat bonus and a role-based bonus. The missing comparison was simple: which plan reduced complaints from part-time staff. Robin marks information on the mockup and changes the next test to ask only the question that could move the bonus design.

Useful information changes the decision; decorative information only postpones responsibility.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Information bias wastes time and can make weak choices feel careful. Readers need a stopping rule that asks whether the next fact can change the live comparison.

reviewCards.front: You want one more report before deciding. What question tests for information bias?
reviewCards.back: Ask what result would change your action. If no result from that report would switch, delay, or reshape the choice, the report is not useful for this decision.

reviewCards.front: A fact could be useful next month but not today. How should you handle it?
reviewCards.back: Separate the decisions by timing. Use the information that answers today's comparison now, and schedule the future data for the future decision.

reviewCards.front: A test result supports your favored diagnosis but does not separate it from the alternative. What is the risk?
reviewCards.back: It may raise certainty without improving discrimination. Useful information must distinguish between the live possibilities, not only make one story feel stronger.

reviewCards.front: What is a stopping rule for gathering more information?
reviewCards.back: A stopping rule names the information that would change the decision before you gather it. Once that information is in or unavailable, you stop collecting decorative facts.

reviewCards.front: A team says more data is always safer. What is the correction?
reviewCards.back: More data is safer only when it changes the relevant comparison. Otherwise it can postpone responsibility and make indecision look careful.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Give every new information request a job. Before gathering more, state the decision, the live options, and the result that would change your action.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I ask for one more report, then I will first write the answer that would change my decision.
If a decision has a deadline, then I will separate information needed now from information useful for the next planning cycle.
If a new fact supports one story but does not separate it from alternatives, then I will look for discriminating evidence instead.
If the group asks for more data, then I will ask what choice remains unresolved and what evidence would resolve it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before your next research request, write two options and the exact finding that would make you switch from one to the other.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review a delayed decision and mark which information changed the action and which information only made the delay feel responsible.
